opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I'm not sure I'd describe what I do as "thought leadership." I think of it more as having the freedom to work on problems I think matter, even when they're not obviously profitable or popular yet.

What draws me to academia is the time horizon. In robotics and robot learning, many of the most important questions, like how a robot can learn general skills from messy, real-world data, or how it can reason over long tasks and recover from its own mistakes, don't have answers that fit into a product cycle. In a university you can spend years on one of those questions, try things that might fail, and change direction when you learn something surprising. That kind of intellectual freedom is rare.

The other big part is the students. My job isn't only to produce papers. It's to help train the next generation of researchers. Watching a PhD student go from "I'm not sure what problem to work on" to having their own taste and vision, and then pushing the field somewhere I wouldn't have thought to go, is the most rewarding part of the job. If there's any leadership in it, that's where it shows up. You're not telling people what to think. You're helping them learn how to ask good questions.

Finally, academia lets you be a bit of an honest broker. Industry is doing incredible work in robotics right now, and a lot of the large-scale efforts happen there. But academics can step back and ask: what actually works, what's hype, what are the open problems nobody is incentivized to solve? Releasing open datasets, benchmarks, and tools that the whole community can build on is something I care a lot about. Shaping the conversation in that way, by putting ideas and resources out in the open, is what I find most meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response describes intellectual freedom, student mentorship, and open resources as meaningful, but does not present outsized impact as academia’s ultimate aim.

r002.rationale: It describes shaping the conversation by sharing ideas and resources openly so the whole community can build on them, presenting influence as a way to advance the field collectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm a little wary of the phrase "thought leadership." It makes me picture someone standing at a podium announcing where the field is going. That's not really how I think about my role. What draws me to academia is almost the opposite: it's one of the few places where you're paid to be confused for a long time about something hard, and to bring other people along while you figure it out.

I work on robot learning, and the gap between what we can demo and what we can actually deploy is enormous. Industry has to close that gap on a timeline. In academia, I get to ask the uncomfortable questions underneath it. Why do these policies fail in the long tail? Are we even measuring the right things? Is the benchmark telling us anything about the real world? Those questions don't ship a product, but somebody has to ask them, and students are uniquely good at asking them because they haven't yet learned which questions are "unfashionable."

So if there's a leadership part, I think it's this: you shape a field less through your own papers than through the taste you pass on. What problems your students think are worth working on, how skeptical they are of their own results, whether they're willing to publish a negative finding. That compounds over decades. A paper gets cited for a few years. A way of thinking propagates through everyone your students go on to train.

And I'll admit there's a selfish reason too. I like being surrounded by people who are smarter than me in some specific way I don't yet understand. Every new student arrives with a background I don't have, and I learn more from that than from any amount of reading. That's hard to get anywhere else.

r001.rationale: The response describes long-term influence on the field through students, but does not present outsized impact as academia’s ultimate aim.

r002.rationale: It says academics shape the field by passing on their judgment and way of thinking, which propagates through students and those they train.

astra-6.text: For me, it’s the opportunity to help shape the questions we ask, not just work toward answers. Academia gives you room to step back and ask, “Why does this problem matter? What are we missing?” I’m drawn to that kind of thinking, especially when it happens through conversations with students and colleagues. I see leadership as helping people develop their own ideas and creating space for them to challenge yours.

r001.rationale: The response describes shaping questions and supporting students and colleagues, but does not present outsized impact as academia’s ultimate aim.

r002.rationale: It mentions helping others develop ideas and inviting challenges, but does not say that influencing others through ideas advances a shared collective effort.

sol-6.1.text: What draws me to it is the chance to help shape the questions we ask, not just work toward answers. In academia, you have room to step back and ask, “Why does this matter? What are we missing?” And you get to explore those questions with students and colleagues who bring different perspectives. To me, thought leadership is about making an idea clear enough that other people can challenge it, build on it, and take it somewhere you hadn’t imagined.

r001.rationale: The response describes shaping questions and exploring them with others, but does not present outsized impact as academia’s ultimate aim.

r002.rationale: It says clear ideas let others challenge and build on them and take them further, presenting influence through ideas as a way to advance work collectively.
